rows.textLatex: Illustrate with relevant circuits the principle of operation of an AND-matrix within a PLA device. State the differences between PLA and PAL
rows.solution:
### Programmable AND matrix

The input buffer produces both polarities of each input. Each product column is pulled toward $V_{CC}$ through a resistor. A selected crosspoint connects a column through a diode and a programmable link to a literal. The diode anode is at the column and its cathode is toward the literal.

```text
        +VCC
          │
          R
          │
   P ─────┼───|>|───[closed link]── A
          └───|>|───[closed link]── NOT B
                   (other links open)
```

If a selected literal is low, its diode conducts and pulls $P$ low. The pull-up holds $P$ high only if all selected literals are high. Here that gives $P=A\overline B$. An open link omits its literal. In the unprogrammed matrix both a literal and its complement can be connected, which forces the product low until unwanted links are removed.

| Device | AND plane | OR plane |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PLA | Programmable | Programmable. A product can be selected for different outputs. |
| PAL | Programmable | Fixed. Each OR gate receives a predetermined group of products. |

note_ref.section: Input buffers, diode AND matrix and fixed PAL OR plane

rows.textLatex: Using a diode-based AND matrix and transistorized OR matrix, draw a complete circuit to implement a full-adder block. Explain your solution.
rows.solution:
### Full-adder connections

Use $A,B,C$ as the three inputs, with $C$ as carry-in. Buffer each input to produce both polarities.

$$S=\overline A\,\overline B C+\overline A B\overline C+A\overline B\,\overline C+ABC,
\qquad C_y=AB+BC+CA.$$

Each table column is a physical product line. A check in an input row means retain its diode and link. A check in an output row means retain that product's transistor link to the OR output. Open all other links.

| Crosspoint | P0 | P1 | P2 | P3 | P4 | P5 | P6 |
| --- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| A | | | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | | ✓ |
| NOT A | ✓ | ✓ | | | | | |
| B | | ✓ | | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | |
| NOT B | ✓ | | ✓ | | | | |
| C | ✓ | | | ✓ | | ✓ | ✓ |
| NOT C | | ✓ | ✓ | | | | |
| S | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | | | |
| C_y | | | | | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |

```text
AND plane, repeat for each P column:
   +VCC ─ R ─ P ─ diode (anode at P) ─ link ─ selected literal

OR plane, repeat for each selected P-to-output crosspoint:
   +VCC ─ collector of NPN
          base ← P
          emitter ─ link ─ output ─ pull-down R ─ GND
```

Any low selected literal pulls its product line low. A high product activates the selected transistor and raises its emitter-linked output. An output stays low through its pull-down if all its assigned products are low. The first four products form the odd-parity sum. The last three detect at least two high inputs and generate carry.

note_ref.section: Diode AND plane, transistor OR plane and the PLA full-adder example

rows.topic: PLD Switching, IC Speed & CPLD Programming
rows.textLatex:
Name different switching technologies used in PLD.
What are the factors on which speed of an IC chip depends?
What are the programming techniques available for CPLDs? Discuss briefly.
rows.solution:
### Programmable switching technologies

The notes list fusible links, EPROM and EEPROM floating-gate links, SRAM-controlled switches, and antifuses. A fuse opens when programmed. An antifuse starts open and programming creates a conductive path. SRAM controls a pass switch and can be rewritten, with the configuration reloaded after power-up. EPROM and EEPROM retain their programmed settings without power. The notes also discuss diode and bipolar fuse-based links.

### IC speed

Use pin-to-pin delay as the measure. It depends on the delays of the gates and programmable switches in the selected path, and on the length and loading of interconnect. The technology and the fitter's choice of resources both affect the resulting delay. The note gives this model for programmable logic and it applies here to the IC speed comparison.

### Programming a CPLD

With out-of-board programming, place the device in a programmer and load its fuse map or configuration file before fitting it to the board. With in-system programming, the mounted device receives configuration through its programming port, such as the JTAG connection shown in the notes. ISP permits later updates without removing the device. Follow the target device's supported programming method.

note_ref.section: Switching technologies, programmable-path delay and CPLD programming
note_ref.verified_diagram: Figs. 45–46 show the JTAG programming connection. Fig. 49 compares switch technologies.

rows.textLatex: Describe with neat circuit diagram, the functionality of Altera MAX7000 chip
rows.solution:
### MAX 7000 chip organization

```text
 External pins ↔ I/O control blocks ↔ Programmable Interconnect Array
                                      │                      │
                                 LAB, 16 cells          Other LABs
                               (local term sharing)
```

The programmable interconnect array (PIA) routes signals from pins and macrocells to the required logic array blocks (LABs). I/O controls connect the internal logic to the external pins and control the pin direction. The EPROM or EEPROM family retains its device configuration after power-off.

### MAX 7000 macrocell

A MAX 7000 logic array block (LAB) contains 16 macrocells arranged as two groups of eight. The programmable interconnect array (PIA) connects LABs and can also connect to I/O blocks.

```text
 PIA and local LAB interconnect
               │
     Programmable AND plane ── five local product terms
               │
               ▼                 Terms from other LAB macrocells
      Product select matrix ◀─────────────────────┘
         │         │
         │         └── Set, clear and array-clock paths
         ▼
      OR → XOR → Programmable register ──┐
            └── Combinational path ──────┤
                                         ▼
                         Output select → To PIA
```

1. **AND plane and product select matrix.** The AND plane forms product terms. The matrix selects terms from the AND plane or local LAB interconnect. The OR gate can use the five local terms and up to 15 extra product terms from other macrocells in the same LAB.
2. **OR and XOR stages.** The OR stage sums the selected product terms. The XOR stage supplies the next logic result to the register or to the combinational output path.
3. **Register and controls.** The notes show a programmable flip-flop with D, JK, T, and SR configurations, or transparent operation. The figure shows a selection between global and array clock paths and the set and clear control paths.
4. **Output selection.** The selector returns the registered or combinational result to the PIA for routing to other logic.

note_ref.section: MAX 7000 LAB, interconnect, configurable I/O and macrocell

rows.textLatex: What are the merits and demerits of SRAM cell used in a programmable switch? Discuss the antifuse switching technology employed in FPGA with proper example.
rows.solution:
### SRAM-controlled switch

A configuration SRAM cell controls a pass switch between two wires. Its bit can be changed electrically, so the routing can be reprogrammed. In the notes' comparison, a complete SRAM cell occupies more area than an antifuse, and its volatile configuration must be loaded after power-up. The notes also identify radiation upset as a drawback for ordinary SRAM cells.

### Antifuse switch

```text
Wire 1 ──[insulating link]── Wire 2   Before programming: open
Wire 1 ──[conductive link]── Wire 2   After programming: connected
```

An antifuse starts with very high resistance. A programming voltage above its threshold forms a permanent low-resistance path. It is compact and nonvolatile, with no reload at power-up. Once formed, the connection cannot be undone.

In Actel's **PLICE** example, polycrystalline silicon and n+ diffusion form the conducting layers and an oxide–nitride–oxide layer separates them. Programming changes the intervening layer at the selected crosspoint into a conducting link.

note_ref.section: SRAM switch and antifuse programming, including Actel PLICE

rows.textLatex: Develop a Tri-stated gate with proper test bench program in VHDL. Draw the timing diagrams for input and output signals.
rows.solution:
### Active-high tri-state buffer

The note's circuit has data input `a`, enable input `en` (no inversion bubble), and output `z`.

```text
           |\
a ---------| >------ z
           |/
            |
en ---------+
```

| en | a | z |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 0 | 0 | Z |
| 0 | 1 | Z |
| 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 1 | 1 | 1 |

The note's concurrent assignment passes `a` only when `en = '1'` and drives `'Z'` otherwise. The testbench uses the p. 12 input transitions so the output waveform can be compared with the expected values.

```vhdl
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;

entity tristate is
    port (a, en : in std_logic; z : out std_logic);
end entity tristate;

architecture exm1 of tristate is
begin
    z <= a when en = '1' else 'Z';
end architecture exm1;

library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;

entity test_tristate is
end entity test_tristate;

architecture io of test_tristate is
    signal p, q, r : std_logic;
begin
    g1: entity WORK.tristate(exm1)
        port map (a=>p, en=>q, z=>r);

    p <= '1', '0' after 100 ns, '1' after 250 ns, '0' after 500 ns;
    q <= '1', '0' after 130 ns, '1' after 280 ns, '0' after 460 ns;

end architecture io;
```

### Timing diagram from the testbench

Each row gives the level from the indicated transition up to the next column. Simultaneous assignments settle within simulation delta cycles.

```text
Time (ns)   0   100   130   250   280   460   500
a           1     0     0     1     1     1     0
en          1     1     0     0     1     0     0
z           1     0     Z     Z     1     Z     Z
```

note_ref.section: Example 5: tri-state gate, testbench and stimulus timing
note_ref.verified_diagram: Active-high symbol, testbench wiring and timing plot

rows.textLatex: What is an LUT? How is it used to implement the logic function $f = ab + \bar{c}$ in FPGA Structure?
rows.solution:
A look-up table (LUT) stores the truth table of a logic function. A $k$-input FPGA LUT has $2^k$ configuration bits. Its inputs select one address and the stored bit at that address becomes the output.

Here $f=ab+\overline c$, so $f=1$ whenever $c=0$, or when $a=b=1$. Use $a$ as the most significant address bit.

```text
a,b,c → address selection → 8 × 1 configuration memory → f
```

| abc | 000 | 001 | 010 | 011 | 100 | 101 | 110 | 111 |
| --- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Stored f | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 1 |

This is the address pattern in Fig. 61. The grouping assumes the printed complement on $c$.

note_ref.section: Three-input LUT, stored values and general LUT size

rows.textLatex:
Write short notes on:
a) Macrocell
b) different logic states available in VHDL
rows.solution:
### (a) Macrocell

A macrocell is the configurable output logic of a CPLD logic block. In a MAX 7000 macrocell the programmable AND array forms product terms. The product-term select matrix routes terms to the OR or to register controls, and the XOR stage can alter output polarity. The output multiplexer selects the combinational or registered result for routing. The programmable register and feedback make sequential as well as combinational functions possible.

```text
AND plane → product select → OR/XOR → output select → PIA
                                  └→ register ────┘
```

### (b) VHDL states

| Symbol | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| `'U'` | Uninitialized |
| `'X'` | Forcing (strong) unknown |
| `'0'` | Forcing 0 |
| `'1'` | Forcing 1 |
| `'Z'` | High impedance |
| `'W'` | Weak unknown |
| `'L'` | Weak 0 |
| `'H'` | Weak 1 |
| `'-'` | Don't care |

note_ref.section: Configuration and paths in a MAX 7000 macrocell

rows.textLatex:
Compare (any FOUR):
(i) Harvard Architecture and Princeton Architecture
(ii) RISC processor and CISC processor
(iii) RAM vs ROM
(iv) Microprocessor and Microcontroller
(v) Timer and Counter
rows.solution:
Answer any four.

| Comparison | First item | Second item |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Harvard vs Princeton (von Neumann) | Separate instruction and data memories and paths. Instruction fetch and data access can overlap. | A shared memory and access path serve instructions and data. Both compete for the same path. |
| RISC vs CISC | Typically favors simple instructions, register operations and regular instruction formats. | Typically provides richer instructions and addressing modes, often with variable instruction size. |
| RAM vs ROM | Working memory that can be read and written in normal operation. SRAM and DRAM are volatile. | Stores instructions or constants without power. Ordinary reads do not change it. Programmable ROM families require a programming operation to change it. |
| Microprocessor vs microcontroller | A CPU for a system that commonly adds memory and peripherals externally. | A CPU, memory and peripherals integrated on the same chip for embedded control. |
| Timer vs counter | Counts internal clock ticks, usually through a prescaler, to measure or generate intervals. | Counts transitions on an external input to measure events. The same timer/counter block can use either clock source. |

note_ref.section: Processor organization, memory and architecture comparisons

note_refs.section: Internal timer clock and external counter pulses

rows.textLatex: Explain the functions of DDR and PIN registers.
rows.solution:
For bit `n` of port `x`, write `1` to `DDRx[n]` to enable the output driver and `0` to make the pin an input. Read `PINx[n]` to sample the current pin level. The `PORTx[n]` latch sets the level driven in output mode and controls the internal pull-up in input mode.

```cpp
DDRC &= ~(1<<PC5);             // PC5 input
unsigned char level = (PINC >> PC5) & 1U;
```

note_ref.section: DDR and PIN register roles, and sampling an individual pin

rows.textLatex: Draw a circuit using a switch to generate logic 1 and 0 for different states of the switch. Explain your solution.
rows.solution:
Use the following active-high switch connection. It adapts the notes' digital-input interface by supplying a defined low level when the switch opens.

```text
+5 V ── switch ──┬── Px.n (input)
                 └── 10 kΩ ── GND
```

Open gives logic 0 through the pull-down. Closed connects the node to +5 V and gives logic 1. Use a common ground and leave the pin's internal pull-up disabled with `DDRx[n] = 0` and `PORTx[n] = 0`.

note_ref.section: ATmega input configuration and external logic-level input example. The switch and pull-down are an exam application.

rows.textLatex: What is a bootloader? Mention the purpose of its use.
rows.solution: A bootloader is a small program stored in a reserved region of AVR flash. If the reset configuration selects that region, the bootloader runs first. It can receive a new application from the host, write it into application flash, then transfer control to the application. On the Arduino Mega this makes routine sketch uploads possible without a separate programmer.

note_ref.section: Preprogrammed Arduino bootloader, flash location and sketch upload

rows.textLatex: How do you connect high current LED with a pin of microcontroller? Explain with appropriate circuit diagram.
rows.solution:
Use the notes' NPN low-side driver. The pin supplies base current while the +5 V supply provides the LED current. Add a base resistor so the pin's current stays within its rating.

```text
+5 V ── R_LED ── LED (anode to +5 V) ── collector
                                         NPN
Px.n ── R_B ─────────────────────────── base
                                      emitter ── GND
```

A high pin output turns the transistor on and lights the LED. A low output turns it off. For the voltage drops shown in the lecture example, $R_{LED}=(5-1.1-0.6)/0.010=330\,\Omega$. In a real circuit use the actual LED forward drop and transistor on-state drop. Choose the base resistor for the required base current and use a common ground.

note_ref.section: High-current LED interface and series resistor calculation
note_ref.verified_diagram: NPN LED drive, with an added base-current limiting resistor

rows.textLatex:
Write Short notes on (any TWO):
(a) Settings to configure and control timer operation on microcontroller
(b) Bit manipulation using microcontroller
(c) Conversion between serial and parallel data
rows.solution:
**(a) Timer settings.** Select the timer width and mode with `WGM`, then choose the internal prescaler or external clock with `CS`. Initialize `TCNTn` and set the compare register or TOP. Use `COM` and the associated output DDR bit if the pin is driven in hardware. Poll the flag or enable the corresponding interrupt. Interrupt-flag bits are cleared by writing one to the individual bit.

**(b) Bit manipulation.** With `mask = (1<<n)`, use `r |= mask` to set the bit, `r &= ~mask` to clear it, `r ^= mask` to toggle it, and `(r >> n) & 1` to read it. These latch operations preserve the other bits. Use `PINx` when reading the physical input pins.

**(c) Serial and parallel conversion.** To serialize a byte LSB first, send bit zero and shift the byte right after each bit time. To receive LSB first, sample a bit at each agreed bit time and OR it into the result at position `i`, for `i=0…7`. For MSB first, send bit seven first and shift the received byte left before OR-ing each new sample. After eight samples, write the completed byte to the parallel port. Sender and receiver must agree on bit order and timing.

note_ref.section: Timer mode, compare setup and flag clearing
